[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Semantic HTML: Understanding and Using Semantic Elements"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction to Semantic HTML"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"Semantic HTML refers to the use of HTML markup to reinforce the semantics, or meaning, of the information in web pages and web applications rather than merely to define its presentation or look. Semantic HTML uses HTML tags to provide meaning to the content within the tag. For example, using the `
` tag to enclose an article makes it clear that the content within is an article."},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Before HTML5, developers often relied heavily on `
` elements with classes and IDs to structure their web pages. While this approach worked, it lacked semantic meaning, making it harder for search engines, assistive technologies, and other developers to understand the content's purpose and structure. HTML5 introduced several new semantic elements to address this issue."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"Benefits of Using Semantic HTML"},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Improved Accessibility: Semantic elements provide better context for screen readers and other assistive technologies, making websites more accessible to users with disabilities."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Better SEO: Search engines can better understand the content and structure of a web page, leading to improved search engine rankings."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Enhanced Code Readability: Semantic elements make the code more readable and maintainable for developers."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Increased Interoperability: Semantic HTML promotes better interoperability between different web technologies and platforms."},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Key Semantic Elements in HTML5"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"Here are some of the most commonly used semantic elements in HTML5:"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"`
